topics.title: People who came and stayed: Jews and Christians

learn.hook: In Kochi, there is a street called Jew Town, and nearby is a synagogue more than 450 years old. How did it get there?
points: Over thousands of years, many groups of people came to India as traders, travellers or people seeking safety. Many settled and became part of Indian society.

Jewish communities have lived in India for many centuries. The Cochin Jews lived in Kerala; the Paradesi Synagogue in Mattancherry, Kochi, was built in 1568. The Bene Israel lived along the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, and Baghdadi Jews settled later in Mumbai and Kolkata.
Jewish communities in India lived peacefully alongside their neighbours and kept their own traditions.

The Syriac (Saint Thomas) Christians of Kerala are among the oldest Christian communities in the world. According to their tradition, Saint Thomas, a disciple of Jesus, reached the Kerala coast in the 1st century CE.
These communities adopted local languages like Malayalam and Marathi, local dress and foods, while keeping their own faiths.

example.q: The Cochin Jews spoke Malayalam, and Syriac Christians in Kerala wear local dress and cook Kerala food. What does this show?
steps: Both groups kept their own faith and prayers.
At the same time, they adopted the language, food and dress of the land.
They became part of Kerala's society while keeping their identity.
example.answer: That communities can keep their own faith while sharing the local culture: they belong to India.

learn.reallife: Kerala's port towns like Kochi and Kodungallur have synagogues, churches, mosques and temples close to one another.

games.title: True or false: early communities
items: The Paradesi Synagogue in Kochi was built in 1568.
It is one of the oldest active synagogues in this part of the world.
The Bene Israel lived along the Konkan coast.
They settled along the coast of Maharashtra.
The Syriac Christians of Kerala are a very recent community.
They are among the oldest Christian communities in the world.
Jewish communities in India adopted local languages.
For example, Cochin Jews spoke Malayalam.
People only came to India in the last 100 years.
Groups have come and settled for thousands of years.

quiz.q: Where is the Paradesi Synagogue?
quiz.explain: It stands in Jew Town, Mattancherry, in Kochi, Kerala.
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with sacred places of other faiths

quiz.q: In which year was the Paradesi Synagogue built?
quiz.explain: It was built in 1568.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a famous date from other history

quiz.q: The Bene Israel Jews lived mainly along the:
quiz.explain: The Bene Israel settled in villages along the Konkan coast.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the regions of different Jewish communities

quiz.q: Which Christian community of Kerala is among the oldest in the world?
quiz.explain: Syriac Christians of Kerala trace their tradition to the 1st century CE.
quiz.mistake: Assumes Christianity arrived only with Europeans

quiz.q: According to tradition, who brought Christianity to Kerala?
quiz.explain: Syriac Christian tradition says Saint Thomas reached Kerala in the 1st century CE.
quiz.mistake: Confuses him with later European visitors

quiz.q: Which language did the Cochin Jews speak in daily life?
quiz.explain: Like their neighbours in Kerala, they spoke Malayalam.
quiz.mistake: Thinks communities kept only their original language

quiz.q: Why did many groups come to India in the past?
options: Because they were forced by Indian kings
For trade, travel or to find safety
quiz.explain: Traders, travellers and people seeking safety came and many settled.
quiz.mistake: Thinks migration had only one reason

quiz.q: What did communities like the Cochin Jews and Syriac Christians do after settling?
options: Kept their faith and adopted local language, food and dress
quiz.explain: They became part of Indian society while keeping their identity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks settling means either complete change or no change

teach.ask: Gappu is a migrant bird! Tell him about some communities who came to India long ago and made it home.
teach.praise: Jews and Syriac Christians made India their home and shared its culture. I feel welcome too!
teach.nudge: Good! Which communities settled in Kerala long ago?

topics.title: Parsis, Arab traders, Siddis and Armenians

learn.hook: A story says that when Parsi refugees reached Gujarat, they promised to mix into society like sugar dissolves in milk, sweetening it without overflowing!
points: The Parsis are Zoroastrians who left Persia (Iran) and, according to their tradition (the Qissa-i-Sanjan), landed at Sanjan in Gujarat, where a local ruler let them settle. They keep their sacred fire burning in fire temples, such as the Iranshah at Udvada.
Parsis have contributed greatly to India: Dadabhai Naoroji, Jamsetji Tata and the scientist Homi J. Bhabha were Parsis.
Arab merchants traded along the Malabar coast for centuries. The Cheraman Juma Masjid at Kodungallur, Kerala, is believed to be one of the oldest mosques in India.

The Siddis are people of African descent who came across the Indian Ocean as sailors, traders and soldiers, and some were brought as slaves. They live in Gujarat, Karnataka and Maharashtra. Malik Ambar, of African origin, became a powerful minister of the Ahmadnagar kingdom.
Armenian traders settled in cities like Kolkata and Chennai. The Armenian Church of Holy Nazareth in Kolkata was built in 1724.

example.q: In the story of the Parsis and the cup of milk, sugar is added to a full cup without making it overflow. What does this story mean?
steps: The full cup of milk stands for the local land and people.
The sugar stands for the Parsi newcomers.
Sugar dissolves and sweetens milk without spilling it: newcomers can blend in and enrich society.
example.answer: That the newcomers would blend in peacefully and make society richer, like sugar in milk.

learn.reallife: Parsi New Year (Navroz), Christmas, Id, Diwali and many other festivals are celebrated in India, and friends often share sweets across communities.

games.title: Community and fact
pairs: Zoroastrians who landed at Sanjan, Gujarat
Minister of Ahmadnagar, of African origin

games.title: Which community?
items: Fire temple at Udvada
Qissa-i-Sanjan
Jamsetji Tata
African descent
Malik Ambar
Church of Holy Nazareth
Traders in Kolkata and Chennai

quiz.q: The Parsis originally came to India from:
quiz.explain: Parsis are Zoroastrians whose ancestors came from Persia.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the origins of different communities

quiz.q: According to Parsi tradition, they first landed at:
quiz.explain: The Qissa-i-Sanjan tells of their landing at Sanjan.
quiz.mistake: Places the Parsi landing on the wrong coast

quiz.q: Which of these was a Parsi?
quiz.explain: The nuclear scientist Homi J. Bhabha was a Parsi, as were Dadabhai Naoroji and Jamsetji Tata.
quiz.mistake: Does not know these famous Parsis

quiz.q: The Cheraman Juma Masjid, believed to be one of India's oldest mosques, is in:
quiz.explain: It is in Kodungallur, on the Malabar coast where Arab traders came.
quiz.mistake: Places it in a later Muslim capital

quiz.q: The Siddis of India are of:
quiz.explain: Siddis trace their ancestry to Africa.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the origins of communities

quiz.q: Malik Ambar was a powerful minister of the:
quiz.explain: Malik Ambar, of African origin, rose to great power in Ahmadnagar.
quiz.mistake: Places him in an ancient empire

quiz.q: The Armenian Church of Holy Nazareth is in:
quiz.explain: It was built in Kolkata in 1724.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up places of different communities

quiz.q: What does the 'sugar in milk' story of the Parsis teach?
options: Newcomers can blend in and enrich society
quiz.explain: The story is a symbol of peaceful blending and contribution.
quiz.mistake: Takes the story literally

teach.ask: Gappu asks about other communities who came to India from far away. Tell him about a few.
teach.praise: Parsis, Arab traders, Siddis and Armenians: all found a home in India. Like sugar in milk!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you tell me about the Parsis or the Siddis?

topics.title: India's pluralism: a home to many

learn.hook: The ancient phrase 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakam' means 'the world is one family'. India has tried to live this idea for centuries.
points: Pluralism means many communities, faiths, languages and customs living together with respect, each keeping its identity.
India is the birthplace of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, and it is also home to Muslims, Christians, Parsis, Jews and many other communities.
India has also given shelter to refugees. In 1959, the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans came to India; Tibetan settlements grew in places like Dharamshala (Himachal Pradesh) and Bylakuppe (Karnataka).
The Constitution protects this pluralism: it gives freedom of religion to all and treats all citizens equally.
Pluralism grows through everyday acts: sharing festivals and food, learning each other's languages and respecting different beliefs.

example.q: Aman, Mary, Gurpreet and Tenzin are classmates. They celebrate Id, Christmas, Gurpurab and Losar, and share sweets with each other. What value do they show?
steps: Each child keeps their own festival and tradition.
They also respect and enjoy each other's festivals.
Living together with respect while keeping one's identity is pluralism.
example.answer: Pluralism: respect for many faiths and cultures living together.

learn.reallife: In many Indian cities you can hear temple bells, the azaan, church bells and gurbani within the same neighbourhood.

games.title: Pluralism: true or false?
items: Pluralism means many communities living together with respect.
Each keeps its identity while respecting others.
India is the birthplace of Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism.
These faiths began in India, as did Hinduism.
The Constitution gives freedom of religion only to some citizens.
Freedom of religion is a Fundamental Right for all.
Many Tibetans came to India in 1959.
They came with the Dalai Lama and settled in many places.
Pluralism means everyone must follow the same customs.
Pluralism respects differences.
'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakam' means 'the world is one family'.
It is an ancient idea of universal kinship.

quiz.q: What does pluralism mean?
options: Many communities living together with respect, each keeping its identity
quiz.explain: Pluralism celebrates diversity with mutual respect.
quiz.mistake: Confuses pluralism with uniformity

quiz.q: 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakam' means:
quiz.explain: It is a Sanskrit phrase meaning the whole world is one family. 'Victory to truth' is Satyameva Jayate.
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with India's national motto

quiz.q: Which of these faiths was born in India?
quiz.explain: Sikhism, like Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism, began in India.
quiz.mistake: Does not know which faiths began in India

quiz.q: In which year did the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans come to India?
quiz.explain: They came to India in 1959.
quiz.mistake: Guesses another famous year

quiz.q: Bylakuppe, a large Tibetan settlement, is in:
quiz.explain: Bylakuppe is in Karnataka; Dharamshala is in Himachal Pradesh.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Tibetans settled only in the Himalayas

quiz.q: How does the Constitution protect pluralism?
options: It gives freedom of religion and equality to all citizens
It gives rights only to the majority
quiz.explain: Freedom of religion and equality are Fundamental Rights for all.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the Constitution with diversity

quiz.q: Which is an everyday act of pluralism?
options: Sharing festival food with neighbours of other faiths
quiz.explain: Small acts of sharing and respect build pluralism.
quiz.mistake: Does not see how daily life shows pluralism

quiz.q: Why is India called 'a home to many'?
options: Everyone in India has the same religion
Nobody has ever moved to India
Many communities, faiths and languages have lived here together for centuries
quiz.explain: India's long history of welcoming and blending many peoples makes it a home to many.
quiz.mistake: Does not see India's diversity

teach.ask: Gappu wonders how so many different people can live together in one country. Explain pluralism to him.
teach.praise: Many people, many faiths, one home, and respect for all. That's India!
teach.nudge: Good! How do people of different faiths live together peacefully?
